Anton thor Helle
an'ton tor hel'le
n. (1683–1748; pastor at Juri and chief translator of the first complete Estonian Bible, 1739)
thor Helle, a Low German surname with the particle thor, at the, and Helle, a place name; Anton, from Latin Antonius.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Anton thor Helle was born in Reval, studied at Kiel, and from 1713 until his death in 1748 was pastor at Juri near Reval and an assessor of the Estonian consistory. He led the team that produced the first complete Bible in Estonian, printed at Reval in 1739 after about fifteen years of work in which the North Estonian dialect he used became the standard written language. He also wrote the grammar that accompanied it and a collection of proverbs and riddles gathered from his own parishioners. The 1739 Bible is the foundation of literate Estonian: a translation made for a peasant congregation, in their own speech, two hundred years after the Reformation had reached their towns. The dictionary records him for the result Scripture promises from exactly that act: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines entrance as the act of entering, the opening or beginning; the simple as the artless, the unlearned, those of plain understanding; and to accomplish as to complete, to fulfil, to perform.

expand to see more

ENTRANCE, n. The act of entering into a place; the opening, passage or avenue by which a place may be entered; beginning, commencement.

SIMPLE, a. Artless; undesigning; sincere; unlearned; weak in intellect; not wise or sagacious.

ACCOMPLISH, v.t. [L. ad and compleo.] To complete; to finish entirely; to execute; to fulfil; to carry into effect.

VOID, a. Empty; vacant; having no effect; null; of no legal force.

UNDERSTANDING, n. The faculty of the human mind by which it apprehends the real state of things presented to it.

Modern Corruption

Pastor at Juri and chief translator of the first complete Estonian Bible, printed at Reval in 1739; his North Estonian became the standard written language.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The entry does have to record a cost honestly. thor Helle's Bible made North Estonian the standard, and in doing so it pushed the South Estonian of Tartu, which had received its own New Testament in 1686, to the margins; a dialect with its own Scriptures became a dialect without a future. That is a real loss, the ordinary price of a standard language, and the dictionary names it rather than celebrating 1739 as pure gain.

The principle to recover is that the Scriptures given to plain people do their own work, and that the work is light and understanding rather than mere literacy. The Psalm locates the effect at the threshold: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). God attaches a guarantee of effect to the word itself and not to the translator's skill — “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11). And even men with the text in their hands need the understanding opened to them by Christ: “Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” (Luk 24:45).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pethach (H6608), an opening or entrance; Hebrew pethi (H6612), the simple.

Hebrew pethach (H6608) — an opening, an entrance, an unfolding; Psalm 119:130.

Hebrew pethi (H6612) — simple, open-minded, easily persuaded; Psalm 119:130.

Hebrew reyqam (H7387) — empty, void, without effect; Isaiah 55:11.

Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to prosper, to succeed; “it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it”, Isaiah 55:11.

Greek dianoigo (G1272) — to open thoroughly, to open the mind; Luke 24:45.

Usage

"“The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130) — the first complete Estonian Bible, Reval 1739."

"“it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — about fifteen years of work with a team of pastors."

"“Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” (Luk 24:45) — a translation made for a peasant congregation."
